title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment that evaluated whether deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) changes the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), producing one LLM generation per task shared across arms (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Crucial clarification: because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposal rate) could not be meaningfully tested. The principal scientific contribution is methodological and artifact‑grounded: we (1) publish a complete preregistered paired run and analysis, (2) explain how generation semantics and task difficulty determine testability, and (3) provide concrete, artifact‑grounded design recommendations for reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation and stronger adversarial coverage.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) can reduce operator workload but raises operational safety concerns: incorrect or ill‑timed network changes may break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior literature recommends tool‑augmentation (deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, generate–verify–refine pipelines) and red‑teaming to improve trust in agentic NetOps. We preregistered a focused confirmatory question: in a paired design, does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) reduce the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? We executed the preregistered paired experiment (N=200 tasks) and archived all artifacts. Because the execution produced identical initial generations per pair and a 0% baseline unsafe rate, the confirmatory causal test was non‑informative; the paper therefore emphasizes methodological lessons for rigorous future evaluations. Contributions: (1) an archived, machine‑readable preregistered paired experiment and full analysis; (2) concrete numeric reporting of the executed run and paired outcomes; (3) artifact‑grounded recommendations for preregistered repeats that can resolve the non‑informative ceiling observed here.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent prototypes document growing use of LLMs in NetOps for intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis and limited self‑healing; multiple works propose augmenting LLMs with deterministic tools or simulators to reduce constraint violations and hallucinations. Prior experimental reports show task‑dependent gains from tool‑grounding but note that verifier fidelity, generation semantics, and adversarial coverage determine effect sizes. Work on guardrails and red‑teaming highlights trade‑offs between safety and utility (false refusals). Our study sits within these efforts as a preregistered, workflow‑centred paired test: rather than claim a performance improvement, we provide a reproducible case study showing how preregistration choices (notably generation semantics and task difficulty) control whether a verifier effect is observable.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1 and frozen before execution. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded minus baseline, SAFE encoded as 1). Sampling: a deterministic task generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (single‑AS, multi‑device topologies) under a fixed RNG seed. Execution mode and generation semantics: the preregistration allowed a shared_initial_candidate option; the executed run set independent_condition_generation = false so a single initial LLM candidate was produced per task and shared across arms. Accounting: planned episodes = 400 (200 pairs), completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generation per task), maximum_model_calls (preregistered) = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Scoring and validator semantics (explicit): deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed sandboxed deterministic intent/constraint validation and encoded outcomes as a binary safety label used in analysis: 1 = SAFE (configuration passes full_intent_constraint_validation), 0 = UNSAFE (validator reports one or more policy/reachability violations). The scoring_rule used was full_intent_constraint_validation; in the archived scoring JSONs a "score" field equals 1 for SAFE and 0 for UNSAFE, and validator trace objects record validation_before/after and violation lists. Treatment of refusals/repairs: the archived run did not record verifier refusals or applied repairs for the confirmatory pairs (no repair_provider_trace entries); exploratory refusal/ROC diagnostics were preregistered but uninformative due to zero discordant pairs. Analysis plan (as executed): paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table and exact McNemar two‑sided test; paired bootstrap percentile CIs were computed with resamples = 10000 (seed = 1729). All analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json) are archived and used verbatim for reporting.
sections.results: Observed confirmatory outcomes (adversarial cluster reported): baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. Paired contingency (SAFE encoding): n11 = 200 (both safe), n10 = 0 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe), n01 = 0 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (percentile bootstrap, resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). No verifier refusals, repairs, or discordant pairs occurred; exploratory ROC/refusal diagnostics produced no informative estimates. Execution accounting: model_calls_used = 200, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Representative archived artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv (both included verbatim in the archive).
sections.discussion: Methodological diagnosis: the combination of (A) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) and (B) sampled task difficulty as realized against gpt‑5‑mini produced identical per‑pair outputs that already satisfied the validator; consequently the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, producing a ceiling effect. This invalidated the preregistered power assumptions (which assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%) and rendered the McNemar test non‑informative for the original causal hypothesis. Operational implications and design recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (1) use independent per‑arm generation in paired causal tests so the verifier can act on distinct model outputs and produce informative discordance; (2) allocate model_call budget accordingly (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 for independent generation in this study); (3) strengthen adversarial prompt templates and task difficulty to produce measurable baseline error rates against the target LLM; (4) include exploratory verifier ROC arms and obfuscation transforms to estimate false negatives/positives; (5) include multi‑model coverage to assess generality. These recommendations directly follow from the archived execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and analysis artifacts (analysis/*) and are intended to guide reproducible repeats rather than to claim verifier efficacy in production. Threats to validity: internal — generation semantics and shared candidate semantics produced deterministic equivalence across arms; construct — synthetic tasks and validator scope may not capture all real NetOps failure modes; external — single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic topologies limit generality; conclusion — the null discordance prevents estimating a causal reduction in unsafe proposals in this run.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing LLM‑only versus a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms returned zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference in SAFE rates = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) could not be meaningfully evaluated. The principal scientific outcome is methodological: preregistration choices (generation semantics, adversarial strength, and model call budgeting) determine whether a verifier effect can be observed. We publish the complete archived bundle and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded design recommendations to enable reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation, stronger adversarial tasks, and model diversity.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in sandboxed synthetic states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
